headline: Halfway Rock holds cod on the slack while the ledges keep bass honest after dark and before dawn
subhead: Casco Bay's cooler water is buying stripers daylight hours the rest of the coast doesn't have — but you still have to find the tide.
body_markdown:
I was out past the Rock Monday morning, engine idling, watching the current lines braid together the way they do about forty minutes before dead slack, and I thought about how little this bay changes from year to year even as everything around it does. Halfway Rock doesn't care what the surface water is doing off Montauk or Sandy Hook. It cares about tide, structure, and bait, in that order, and this week it delivered on two of the three.

Groundfish first, since that's where the discipline pays off. I fished the northeast side of the Rock in 70 to 90 feet on the last hour of the ebb into slack, diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, and connected on cod in the 4 to 8 pound range, with one better fish that pulled hard enough to make me second-guess my drag setting before I got a look at him — call it 12 pounds, released clean. Haddock have been scattered rather than schooled; I marked a few pods on the sounder holding tight to bottom but they weren't feeding hard, which tells me the bait — likely herring fry and small pollock — hasn't concentrated yet the way it will once the tide swings build back toward full moon. That's worth watching over the next week. The slack window at Halfway Rock is short, maybe twenty minutes on either side of the change, so if you're marking fish and not getting bit, don't burn line waiting them out — reposition and try the drop on the western ledge instead.

Bass have been the more interesting story, and here's where Casco Bay is doing something different than the rest of the coast right now. Farther south, from New Jersey through southern New England, stripers have gone essentially nocturnal — surface water's sitting in the low-to-mid seventies and the fish are holding deep on structure until dark. We don't have that problem yet. Our water's still cool enough — I'm reading mid-to-upper sixties around the mouth of the Presumpscot and off Peaks Island — that bass are willing to work the ledges in daylight, provided you're fishing the right stage of tide. Bailey Island's back side, the ledges off Mackerel Cove, has been giving up slot fish on the incoming, an hour either side of the tide change, on 3/4-ounce chartreuse bucktails worked slow along bottom, occasionally on live mackerel when we could get them to stay on the hook. Cape Small's river mouth — where the New Meadows dumps warmer, baitfish-rich water into cooler bay water — has produced some of the better numbers this week, fish up to 30 inches on topwater at first light before the sun gets high and pushes them down onto the drop-off. Harpswell's ledges have been quieter, more of a one-or-two-fish morning, but the quality's been decent when they show.

Mackerel are thinning out, which is normal for this point in the season — the big May and June runs have mostly pushed offshore or dispersed, but there are still pockets working the Portland breakwater and the backside of Peaks Island in the early morning, small jigs on a Sabiki rig, fish running 10 to 12 inches. If you need bait for the bass or the cod trip, that's still your best bet, just don't expect the density we had two months ago.

The surprise this week — and it's a small one, worth mentioning because it's unusual for this bay — has been a few bluefish showing up around the mouth of Casco Bay proper, inside of Two Lights. Warm year, warmer than most, and it's pulled a few blues north of their usual range. Nothing like the blitzes you'd see from bunker schools farther south, just occasional fish in the 3 to 5 pound class mixed in with the bass on topwater plugs. I wouldn't plan a trip around them, but if you're working the ledges off Two Lights on a moving tide, don't be shocked if something with a sharper set of teeth than a striper hits your plug.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect steady, typical mid-summer Maine conditions through the stretch, and that's exactly what's held. Warm, stable air, water temperatures cool enough to keep the bass working daylight tides, groundfish holding tight to structure at Halfway Rock. No surprises, which in this business is its own kind of good news.

Looking ahead, the moon's waxing toward full in the first week of August, which should sharpen current through the bay's rips and channels — Halfway Rock, the mouth of the New Meadows, the gut between Peaks and House Island. Stronger current usually means better bait concentration, and better bait concentration usually means the haddock I've been marking but not hooking start feeding in earnest. If I had one morning to fish next week, I'd take the last of the ebb at the Rock for groundfish, then run into Cape Small on the incoming for bass before the sun climbs too high. Watch the wind — if it swings southwest and holds, the bay can get a light chop that makes the ledge work sloppy, and I'd rather fish a clean tide than fight a messy one.
